rv.q: "The Unbelievers" is more realistically frightening than any of those others.

The play's almost clinical approach to the investigation and its impact on the family has an admirable forensic authenticity, but Miriam's anguish is left so little explored that her plight never becomes particularly affecting or illuminating.
Her laserlike focus on finding the truth cuts through an otherwise stilted and overwrought play.
The Unbelievers is a moving, haunting, and theatrical dramatization of a traumatic real life issue.
The Unbelievers is a deeply affecting piece about a woman slowly unwinding and a family desperately trying to keep her, and themselves, together. And with Ambrose as the lead, it's unmissable.

Payne's adept writing, which often blurs genre and places tight comedy against deep pathos, and Knud Adams's skillful, confident direction place us inside Miriam's mind, and the result is a stunning piece of theatre likely to stick in your own.
If you're not sobbing (openly or silently) – whether you're a parent or not – as these words are spoken by Ambrose, perhaps you aren't alive.
The Unbelievers does boast one crowning achievement: the red-haired Lauren Ambrose.
Lauren Ambrose gives a tour d'force performance that swept me away in its all-encompassing embrace of absolute terror.

While The Unbelievers proves unconvincing as a domestic drama, it offers a riveting character study of a woman who responds to an unthinkable situation in the only way she knows how, all others be damned.
It's just that it seemed like it could have been a very good or even excellent play before settling into one that's just fine.

cn.t: Critics mostly praise this shattering family drama about a missing child, with Lauren Ambrose earning raves for her devastating performance, though some find Payne's non-linear storytelling confusing and emotionally distant.

vr.q: The Unbelievers had me mostly on the edge of my seat with its compelling premise and even more compelling ensemble work.
